title: Zoom Video Conferencing: Complete Architecture
description: Design a global low-latency video conferencing platform with WebRTC signaling, Selective Forwarding Units (SFUs), Simulcast, and cascading media routing.

data.text: Design a real-time global video conferencing system at Zoom scale. The system supports 300+ million daily meeting participants hosting calls ranging from 1-on-1 chats to 1,000-person all-hands webinars. The paramount technical challenge is ultra-low latency interactive media delivery: packet latency must remain under 150ms globally over UDP, video must dynamically adapt to jitter and variable bandwidth (Simulcast/SVC), media streams must be efficiently routed across Selective Forwarding Units (SFUs) without server-side video transcoding melting CPU capacity, and calls must withstand up to 25% packet loss without audio dropouts.

terms.definition: A media routing server that inspects incoming RTP packets and forwards them to appropriate participants without decoding or re-encoding video frames.
The sending client encodes and uploads video at multiple resolutions/bitrates simultaneously (e.g. 180p, 360p, 720p), allowing the SFU to route the optimal layer to each viewer.
The out-of-band communication channel (over WebSocket or HTTPS) used to exchange SDP session parameters, codecs, and ICE network candidates.
NAT traversal protocols: STUN discovers public IP/port bindings; TURN acts as a fallback media relay server when symmetric NAT blocks direct P2P/SFU UDP.
The SFU analyzes audio packet volume levels to switch the dominant high-resolution video stream to the speaking participant.

data.title: Functional Requirements
items: Meeting Lifecycle: Create, schedule, join with meeting ID/passcode, host controls (mute, kick, lock)
Multi-Party Audio & Video: Up to 1,000 active participants with gallery view (25-49 tiles) and speaker view
Screen Sharing & In-Meeting Chat: Low-framerate high-resolution screen transmission with real-time text chat
Dynamic Bandwidth Adaptation: Degrade video resolution smoothly during network congestion without dropping audio
Cloud Recording: Record gallery view, speaker view, and separate audio stems with cloud storage export
Breakout Rooms: Split active call into sub-sessions and merge back seamlessly

data.title: Non-Functional Requirements
items: Ultra-Low Latency: Glass-to-glass (camera to screen) latency under 150ms round-trip time (RTT)
Scale: 300M+ daily participants; millions of concurrent active rooms worldwide
Packet Loss Resilience: Clear audio at up to 25-30% packet loss using Forward Error Correction (FEC)
CPU Efficiency: SFUs route raw UDP/RTP packets without transcoding to support thousands of streams per box
High Availability: 99.99% reliability with automatic migration of meetings if a media server fails

data.text: Zoom separates the Control Plane (Signaling, Authentication, Meeting Scheduling) from the Data Plane (Cascading SFU Multimedia Routers operating over raw UDP/RTP).

data.text: To establish a video call, the client connects to the Signaling Gateway, receives an assigned SFU media server close to their geographic location, and exchanges Session Description Protocol (SDP) configurations.

data.text: Video Architecture Comparison: Mesh vs MCU vs SFU

rows: Great for 1-on-1 (WhatsApp/FaceTime), impossible for group meetings
Excessive: Server decodes & re-encodes all video into 1 frame
Legacy telecom (Polycom/Cisco); expensive and adds high latency
Balanced: Client uploads 1 simulcast, downloads N streams
Ultra-Low: Server simply routes packets without transcoding
Modern gold standard (Zoom, Google Meet, Teams, Discord)

faqs.question: Why does Zoom use UDP instead of TCP for media streaming?
faqs.answer: TCP guarantees delivery via retransmissions (ACK/NACK). If a packet drops over TCP, subsequent packets wait (head-of-line blocking), causing frozen frames and 1-2 second audio lag. In live human conversation, a late video frame is useless. UDP with RTP transmits packets without blocking; missing packets are masked using Forward Error Correction (FEC) or packet loss concealment (PLC).

faqs.question: How does Simulcast save client download bandwidth in a 50-person call?
faqs.answer: If 50 people are on a call, a participant viewing gallery view (5x5 grid) only needs tiny 180p thumbnails. The SFU dynamically drops the 720p and 360p layers and only forwards the 180p stream for background attendees. Only the person actively speaking has their 720p layer forwarded, slashing client downstream bandwidth by over 80%.

faqs.question: What is a Cascading SFU architecture and why is it needed for global calls?
faqs.answer: If a meeting has attendees in New York, London, and Tokyo, routing every participant to a single US data center introduces 200ms+ transatlantic delay for Asian and European members. With cascading SFUs, European attendees connect to a local London SFU; Asian attendees connect to Tokyo. The SFUs bridge together over dedicated high-speed cloud backbones, sending only 1 copy of each stream across continents.

faqs.question: How does Active Speaker Detection prevent switching jitter?
faqs.answer: SFUs monitor voice activity and audio energy levels in the Opus audio packets. To prevent the active speaker view from flashing frantically when someone coughs or says "uh-huh", the algorithm applies hysteresis (a minimum speech duration threshold of ~500ms before switching focus) and audio ducking.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Selective Forwarding Units (SFUs) inspect and forward UDP/RTP packets without expensive video transcoding
Simulcast allows clients to upload multiple quality streams so the SFU can match bandwidth per viewer
Control Plane (WebSockets/HTTPS for SDP signaling) is strictly isolated from Data Plane (UDP media traffic)
Cascading SFUs bridge regional media clusters across global dedicated backbones to keep local RTT under 150ms
Active speaker detection monitors audio packet energy with hysteresis smoothing to spotlight the primary presenter
data.takeaway: Zoom delivers real-time interactive video at massive scale by routing lightweight UDP packets through distributed SFU clusters, pairing Simulcast and active speaker detection to optimize every participant's bandwidth.
